_readme.purpose: Every story in the collection, in the order it enters the shelf. wave 1 = the famous ones that earn trust. wave 2 = the deep cuts that earn the subscription. wave 3 = the difficult ones, restored on Rama's call, gated rather than cut.
_readme.the_gate: audience.gated is the mechanism that makes 'parent's discretion' real rather than a slogan. A gated story never surfaces as tonight's pick and never appears in browse until the parent switches on 'Include the difficult ones', and its careNote is shown before the first line. Nothing is removed from the collection; the parent chooses when.
_readme.counts: 76 stories — wave 1: 30 · wave 2: 30 · wave 3: 8 · wave 4: 9 · gated: 5
_readme.wave_4: The gaps, found by asking which nights of the year the collection could not speak to. No Devi cycle and no story of Rama coming home meant Navaratri and Diwali had nothing between them. Also thickens the character map: mothers, Ravana's family, and Ayodhya beyond Rama.

canon.title: The Squirrel Who Carried Sand
canon.locus: Yuddha Kāṇḍa — the building of the Setu
canon.value: small things count
canon.hook: An army throws mountains into the sea. Nobody notices the squirrel with sand in her fur.

canon.title: Śabarī's Tasted Berries
canon.value: love outranks correctness
canon.hook: She bites every berry first to check it is sweet, which ruins it. He eats them anyway.

canon.title: Jāmbavān Reminds Hanumān
canon.value: you need someone to remind you
canon.hook: Hanumān says nothing while everyone measures how far they can jump. Then Jāmbavān reminds him who he is.

canon.title: Guha Keeps Watch
canon.value: friendship across rank
canon.hook: Guha offers Rāma a kingdom. Rāma asks for only one thing: feed my father's horses.

canon.title: Jaṭāyu's Last Flight
canon.value: doing what you can when help is far away
canon.hook: Rāvaṇa is carrying Sītā away. Rāma is far away. One old bird decides to stop him alone.

canon.title: Śravaṇa and the Two Baskets
canon.value: carrying the people who carried you
canon.hook: A boy carries both his parents across the country on a pole. Then an arrow finds him at the river.

canon.title: The Line Lakṣmaṇa Drew
canon.locus: Not in Vālmīki. Rāmcaritmānas and later folk tradition
canon.value: how a story grows a new part
canon.hook: Vālmīki does not narrate a line at Sītā's hut. Later Rāmāyaṇa traditions speak of one; this story will name the telling it follows.

canon.title: The Tail Bhīma Could Not Lift
canon.value: strength meets its match, politely
canon.hook: The strongest man alive cannot move an old monkey's tail off the path. So he stops, bows, and asks who is in front of him.

canon.title: The Eye of the Bird
canon.locus: Ādi Parva, Sambhava Parva, K.M. Ganguli sections CXXXIV–CXXXV
canon.value: what attention actually is
canon.hook: A teacher asks each prince what he can see. Only one answer keeps getting smaller.

canon.title: The Last Morsel in the Pot
canon.value: one grain is enough
canon.hook: Ten thousand guests are bathing before their meal. Draupadī has already eaten, and her vessel will give no more food today.
canon.careNote: The family fears a visiting sage's anger. Do not turn the rescue into a promise that faith prevents hunger or hardship.

canon.title: The Crane at the Lake
canon.value: answering honestly under pressure
canon.hook: Four brothers drink and fall. The fifth is asked what the greatest wonder in the world is, and gets it right.

canon.title: Karṇa Gives Away His Armour
canon.locus: Vana Parva, K.M. Ganguli sections CCC and CCCVIII; birth notice Ādi Parva CXI
canon.value: giving when it costs everything
canon.hook: Karṇa is warned exactly what Indra will ask for. When the request comes, he gives anyway.

canon.title: Ekalavya's Thumb
canon.value: there is no clean moral here
canon.hook: A forest boy teaches himself archery from a clay statue of the teacher who turned him away. Then the teacher comes to collect.

canon.title: Abhimanyu and the Spiral
canon.value: being sent in by people who knew
canon.hook: He learned how to get into the formation before he was born. Nobody finished telling him how to get out.

canon.title: The Mountain Held Up by Sticks
canon.value: letting others help
canon.hook: A seven-year-old holds a hill over a village for seven days. A cowherd puts his stick up to help.

canon.title: The Rope That Was Two Fingers Short
canon.value: you cannot tie love with a short rope
canon.hook: Yaśodā joins another rope to the first. Then another. The ends still will not meet.
canon.careNote: A mother chases her child with a stick, puts it aside, and binds him to a mortar. Tell the devotional episode without presenting restraint as parenting advice.

canon.title: Dhruva Stands Still
canon.value: a child who would not be told no
canon.hook: He is told he cannot sit on his father's lap. He is five. He walks into the forest instead, and becomes a star.

canon.title: Gajendra Lets Go
canon.value: when your own strength runs out
canon.hook: The strongest elephant in the forest pulls against a crocodile for a thousand years, and then stops pulling.

canon.title: Sudāmā's Handful of Rice
canon.value: the friend who could not ask
canon.hook: He walks for days to see his rich old schoolfriend, carrying a knotted rag of beaten rice he is ashamed of.

canon.title: Whoever Drinks the Poison First
canon.value: there is no nectar without the poison
canon.hook: Gods and asuras churn the sea for the drink that ends death. The first thing that comes up is poison.

canon.title: Prahlāda and the Pillar
canon.value: saying it in a dangerous house
canon.hook: A boy keeps giving the wrong answer in his father's classroom, and his father is a king who does not lose.

canon.title: Gaṇeśa Goes Around the World
canon.value: what counts as the world
canon.hook: Gaṇeśa never went around the world. He won the race anyway.

canon.title: Bharata and the Fawn
canon.value: the cost of one small love
canon.hook: A king gives up a kingdom without blinking, then loses everything again over an orphaned deer he cannot stop watching.

canon.title: The Boy Who Waited Three Nights
canon.value: refusing an easy answer
canon.hook: Death offers a boy the whole earth if he will only stop asking one question. The boy says no.

canon.title: The Chariot
canon.value: who is holding your reins
canon.hook: You are a chariot. Your senses are the horses, and somebody in there is supposed to be driving.

canon.title: Śvetaketu and the Salt
canon.value: the invisible thing that is everywhere
canon.hook: His father drops salt into water and asks him to bring it back the next morning. He cannot.

canon.title: The Seed Śvetaketu Opened
canon.value: the tree you cannot see
canon.hook: His father asks him to break a banyan fruit, and then one tiny seed. What can he see inside?
canon.careNote: The unseen essence is a philosophical teaching, not a claim that a seed contains nothing or a substitute for botany.

canon.title: Satyakāma Says the Hard Thing
canon.value: saying the thing you dreaded saying
canon.hook: A boy is asked his family name at the school gate, and has to say the one thing he was hoping not to.

canon.title: The Gods Who Could Not Burn a Blade of Grass
canon.value: borrowed power
canon.hook: Fire is asked to burn one straw. Wind is asked to move it. Neither of them can, and both are very embarrassed.

canon.title: Two Birds on One Tree
canon.value: the one who eats and the one who watches
canon.hook: Two birds sit on the same branch. One eats the fruit. The other just watches him eat it.

canon.title: The Temple Nobody Could See
canon.value: care spent where nobody is looking
canon.hook: A poor man builds a temple entirely in his head. On the day it is finished, a king has to move his own festival.

canon.title: The Loincloth on the Scales
canon.value: keeping a promise past where it hurts
canon.hook: A merchant piles cloth, gold and jewels onto a balance. One small loincloth still outweighs everything.

canon.title: The Old Man with the Deed
canon.locus: Taḍuttāṭkoṇḍa Purāṇam — wedding, deed, Tiruveṇṇainallūr assembly, temple revelation and first hymn
canon.value: losing an argument you were sure of
canon.hook: An old man stops a wedding with a palm-leaf deed. The groom calls the claim impossible, follows him to court—and loses.
canon.careNote: The hagiography uses a hereditary-servitude deed as its legal device. We say plainly that this is not an argument for one human being owning another.

canon.title: Nandanār and the Bull
canon.value: a rule that did not move
canon.hook: A man who is not allowed inside the temple stands outside for years. The stone bull in the doorway is what moves.

canon.title: The Second Mango
canon.value: a guest fed before the household
canon.hook: Two mangoes came to the house. She gave one away. Now her husband is home and wants the second one, and it is very good.

canon.title: Appar's Small Spade
canon.locus: Tirunāvukkaracar Purāṇam, temple-service and Tiruppukalūr testing sequence, especially verses 1681–1683
canon.value: choosing the smallest job on purpose
canon.hook: A poet-saint clears weeds from temple ground. Gold and jewels appear in the earth, and he keeps working.

canon.title: Three in a Doorway
canon.work: Mudhal Tiruvantāti, with the commentators' account
canon.value: room made where there was none
canon.hook: A doorway with space for one man to lie down. Then two to sit. Then three to stand. Then someone else pushes in, in the dark.

canon.title: The Highwayman's Last Robbery
canon.work: Śrīvaiṣṇava Guruparamparā traditions; compare Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār's Periya Tirumoḻi
canon.locus: Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār caritam — roadside robbery and mantra-conversion episode; Periya Tirumoḻi 1.1.1–10 as earlier poetic witness
canon.value: being caught by what you stole
canon.hook: A highwayman strips a wedding party of its jewels, then finds one ring he cannot remove and a bundle he cannot lift.

canon.title: Carried In on Someone’s Shoulders
canon.locus: Divya Sūri Caritam and the Guruparamparā Prabhāvam
canon.value: what you do to him you do to me
canon.hook: A temple priest throws a stone at a singer who does not hear him. That night the Lord tells the priest in a dream to bring him in; when the singer refuses, the priest offers his own shoulders.

canon.title: The King Who Kept Setting Off for Laṅkā
canon.work: Śrīvaiṣṇava Guruparamparā traditions; compare Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār's Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi
canon.locus: Kulaśēkhara Āḻvār caritam — Rāmāyaṇa-recitation and army-march episode; Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi decads 8–10 as earlier Rāma-centred poetic witness
canon.value: being properly inside a story
canon.hook: The reciter reaches a moment when Rāma is badly outnumbered. King Kulaśēkhara stands up and orders his own army to march.

canon.title: Āṇḍāḷ Wears It First
canon.value: what a person wants unprompted
canon.hook: Her father makes the garland for the god every morning. She has been trying it on first, and today he sees her do it.

canon.title: Sixteen Years Without a Word
canon.work: Divya Sūri Caritam and the Guruparamparā Prabhāvam
canon.locus: The life of Nammāḻvār and of Madhurakavi Āḻvār
canon.value: a question worth a long walk
canon.hook: A baby who never cried, never fed, never spoke, sitting in a hollow tree for sixteen years. Then a stranger asks him one question and he answers it.

canon.title: What Was Under the Cloth
canon.value: an argument nobody needed to have
canon.hook: Two crowds arrive to claim the body of a man who spent his life telling them they were the same. They lift the cloth.

canon.title: Mīrā and the Cup
canon.value: not stopping when told to
canon.hook: Her family sends her a cup and asks her to drink it in front of them. She sings first, which is the part they had not planned for.

canon.title: The Bill Nobody Would Honour
canon.value: vouching for someone with nothing
canon.hook: A poor poet writes a note promising pilgrims their money in Dvārakā. He has no money in Dvārakā. He has no money anywhere.

canon.title: Who Was Helping Janābāī
canon.work: Mahīpati, Bhaktavijaya; Janābāī's abhaṅgas as parallel witness
canon.locus: Bhaktavijaya chapter 21, ovis 49–118, the grinding episode
canon.value: the work nobody watches
canon.hook: At the mill before dawn, Viṭṭhal turns the stone beside Janābāī. When Goṇābāī comes to see who is helping, the blow she aims at Janābāī lands on the visitor.
canon.careNote: Goṇābāī suspects Janābāī of hiding a helper and missing flour, and strikes at her with a cane; the blow lands on Viṭṭhal. The later pendant accusation is outside this telling but follows in the same source chapter.

canon.title: Neither of Them Found the End
canon.value: the cost of one small lie
canon.hook: A column of fire takes in two terrible weapons. One god searches below, another flies above, and a falling flower is asked to witness something it never saw.
canon.careNote: The two gods launch dangerous weapons. Near the end, an attendant seizes Brahmā’s fifth head and raises a sword, but Śiva stops him before the blow.

canon.title: The Hand That Burned Whatever It Touched
canon.value: asking for the wrong thing
canon.hook: He asks for a boon: whatever he puts his hand on turns to ash. It is granted immediately, and the first thing he reaches for is the one who granted it.

canon.title: When Rāvaṇa Shook Kailāsa
canon.locus: Uttara Kāṇḍa, sarga 16, the shaking of Kailāsa and the naming of Rāvaṇa
canon.value: a villain who is not only that
canon.hook: A flying chariot stops at Śiva’s mountain. Rāvaṇa decides to move the mountain itself, until one toe presses down.

canon.title: Pārvatī and the Visitor Who Questioned Her Choice
canon.value: deciding, and not being talked out of it
canon.hook: An aged ascetic comes to Pārvatī's place of tapas and questions why she seeks Śiva. She answers what he cannot see in Śiva's outward form, then discovers who has come to visit.

canon.title: Rantideva Gives Away the Water
canon.value: giving from the bottom
canon.hook: Forty-eight days without food. The meal finally arrives. Then someone knocks, and then someone else, and then a dog.

canon.title: Bhagīratha Waits for the River
canon.value: finishing what three generations started
canon.hook: The river is caught in Śiva’s hair, then swallowed by a sage. A king keeps going because sixty thousand ancestors still wait for her water.
canon.careNote: The story begins with the ashes of sixty thousand ancestors and ends when the river’s water releases them. Their deaths are recounted, not shown.

canon.title: Two Lights in the Anthill
canon.locus: Vana Parva, Tīrtha-yātrā Parva, sections CXXII–CXXIII in Ganguli's translation
canon.value: the choice you make on purpose
canon.hook: Sukanyā touches two lights in an anthill with thorns. Only afterward does she learn who was inside.
canon.careNote: Sukanyā unknowingly injures a sage's eyes. He then demands that her father give her to him in marriage before he will forgive the family. The telling keeps that pressure visible; it does not call the marriage her free choice.

canon.title: The Child on the Banyan Leaf
canon.value: being very small on purpose
canon.hook: The sage outlives the end of the world. He swims in the empty water for a long time, and then finds a baby asleep on a leaf.
canon.careNote: The world ends and he is the only one left in it, frightened and alone in the water for a long time. Nobody dies where the child can see it, and the world is there again at the end.

canon.title: What the Earth Agreed To
canon.value: asking instead of taking
canon.hook: The earth has stopped giving anything and the king raises his bow. She turns into a cow and runs, and then stops and makes him a counter-offer.

canon.title: The Rāmāyaṇa Where Rāvaṇa Is a Good King
canon.value: the same story told another way
canon.hook: In this one Rāvaṇa is not a demon, does not have ten heads, never harms Sītā — and is still the one who loses everything.
canon.note: Shelved 2026-09-10 — Vālmīki is the authority here; a good-king Rāvaṇa confuses rather than widens. Draft kept in content/shelved/.

canon.title: Hanumān Wrote One Too
canon.locus: The traditional account of how the play came to exist
canon.value: letting the better one go
canon.hook: Vālmīki discovers Hanumān wrote a better Rāmāyaṇa than his. Hanumān throws it into the sea.

canon.title: Gaṇeśa's One Condition
canon.value: buying yourself time to think
canon.hook: He will write down the whole Mahābhārata, but only if the dictation never stops. So Vyāsa starts hiding knots in it.

canon.title: The Word Given from the Shrine
canon.value: receiving a beginning for a great work
canon.hook: Asked to write the saints' lives, Sēkkiḻār prays at Chidambaram. A later life tradition tells how the opening word was given to him.

canon.title: Kaṇṇappar Gives What He Has
canon.value: giving the thing you cannot spare
canon.hook: A hunter who knows nothing about worship brings meat and river-water in his mouth. When the stone eye starts to bleed, he works out what to do about it with the only tools he has.
canon.careNote: He takes out his own eye and reaches for the second. Told for its tenderness, not its shock — the act is one line, and the story does not linger on it. Many Tamil families tell this at six; we set it at eleven and gate it, because a child who has not been raised on it hears self-injury before devotion.

canon.title: Siṟuttoṇḍar
canon.value: a vow taken past the end of reason
canon.hook: A guest will only eat one dish, and names it. The couple do not argue, and do not hesitate, and that is the part that has unsettled listeners for a thousand years.
canon.careNote: A father and mother kill and cook their own child to feed a guest, who then returns the child alive. The hardest thing in the entire corpus. Read it yourself before you read it to anyone. The story's own point is that the vow was monstrous and was honoured anyway — that ambiguity is the reason it survived, and flattening it into a moral does it no favours.

canon.title: Kōṭpuli's Granary
canon.value: a rule kept when it should have bent
canon.hook: A soldier comes home from a long campaign to find his family alive, and the grain he had set aside for the temple gone.
canon.careNote: He kills relatives who used grain set aside for temple offerings during a famine. The deaths are not undone; the Periya Purāṇam says Śiva grants them heaven. This story needs an adult ready to discuss the harm without treating it as an example to follow.

canon.title: Iyaṟpagai Says Yes
canon.value: a promise with no exceptions in it
canon.hook: He has vowed to give any devotee whatever they ask for. A stranger asks for his wife; he agrees before telling her, and she says she has no choice but to obey.
canon.careNote: He promises his wife to a stranger without asking her first. She says she has no choice but to obey; opposing relatives are killed. The text later grants them heaven, but neither her constrained response nor those deaths should be softened. Ask whether a promise that costs someone else was his to make.

canon.title: The Sacrifice Nobody Was Invited To
canon.value: a slight that could not be let go
canon.hook: Dakṣa holds a great sacrifice without inviting his daughter Satī's husband. She goes despite Śiva's warning and confronts her father there.
canon.careNote: Satī dies at her father's sacrifice and Śiva's grief levels it. Family humiliation, a daughter's death, a beheading. Big and operatic rather than gruesome, but it is a story about a parent doing real harm — which for some children lands harder than a battlefield.

canon.title: The Jar Above the Cot
canon.work: Pañcatantra, Pūrṇabhadra recension in Arthur W. Ryder's translation
canon.locus: Book V, The Brahman's Dream (embedded tale following Slow, the Weaver)
canon.value: the daydream that breaks the pot
canon.hook: A brahmin dreams that a jar of barley-meal will become a house, a family and a fortune. His foot reaches the jar first.
canon.careNote: In a daydream, the brahmin imagines kicking his future wife when she does not respond to him. No wife or child exists in the scene, and the actual kick breaks his own jar. The telling does not present violence toward her as a joke or a solution.

canon.title: The Howl Beneath the Blue
canon.locus: Book I, The Blue Jackal, pp. 122–125 (embedded tale)
canon.value: the thing you cannot help doing
canon.hook: The forest animals bow to a strange blue creature. Then a pack of jackals begins to howl.
canon.careNote: Dogs attack a jackal; he deceives the forest animals, and a tiger kills him when exposed. The death is brief and non-graphic. Do not invite approval of the killing or turn animal kinship into a lesson about human birth.

canon.title: When Mice Ate Iron
canon.value: answering a lie in its own language
canon.hook: A merchant asks for his iron balance back. His friend says mice ate it. Soon the friend hears an equally impossible claim.
canon.locus: Book I, The Mice That Ate Iron, pp. 192–195 (embedded tale)
canon.careNote: A merchant confines a fifteen-year-old boy in a cave to pressure the boy's father. The boy is returned. Do not treat using a child as leverage as admirable or safe to imitate.

canon.title: The Buffalo Nobody Could Fight
canon.value: made out of what everyone had left
canon.hook: No god can beat him alone, so they each give up a piece of what they have, and out of the pile something walks that none of them expected.

canon.title: The Woman Who Fed the World
canon.value: feeding people before explaining anything
canon.hook: A hundred years without rain. She arrives with vegetables growing out of her own body, and hands them out before she says a word.

canon.title: Śiva Goes Begging at His Own Door
canon.value: who actually feeds you
canon.hook: Śiva says the world — and food — are an illusion. Annapūrṇā turns the kitchens off. Soon he appears with a bowl.

canon.title: The Foot She Almost Stepped On
canon.value: stopping when you have won
canon.hook: Kālī has won and cannot stop. Śiva lies down in her path and waits to see whether she looks down.

canon.title: The Night They Lit the Whole Road
canon.locus: Yuddha Kāṇḍa — the return to Ayodhyā
canon.value: coming home
canon.hook: Rāma is coming home after fourteen years. Nobody knows exactly when, so Ayodhyā lights the whole road and waits.

canon.title: The Morning After Naraka
canon.value: the mercy nobody had to give
canon.hook: Narakāsura asks for one thing as he dies: remember this day as a festival, not as his defeat. We still do.

canon.title: The Empty Chair
canon.value: what you were handed without asking
canon.hook: Bharata is handed a kingdom he never asked for. He walks into the forest to give it back — and returns with Rāma's sandals.

canon.title: Vibhīṣaṇa Comes Across the Sky
canon.value: vouching for someone with nothing
canon.hook: Rāvaṇa's brother appears over Rāma's camp asking for refuge. The camp thinks he may be a spy.

canon.title: The Last Errand Before the War
canon.value: trying anyway when you have been told
canon.hook: He goes to ask for five villages instead of a kingdom, knowing the answer, because nobody afterwards should be able to say it was not asked.

canon.title: The First Poem Was an Accident
canon.value: grief that turns into something
canon.hook: Vālmīki goes to the river to bathe. He returns having spoken the first poem — without meaning to write one.

canon.title: The Garland Indra Did Not Get Down For
canon.value: what you stop noticing
canon.hook: Indra accepts a sage's gift without getting off his elephant. That small discourtesy is how the world loses its luck.

canon.title: Everyone Told Her to Be Sensible
canon.value: deciding, and not being talked out of it
canon.hook: A mountain's daughter decides who she will marry. Everyone argues her out of it — and then the man himself turns up in disguise to argue, and he is the one who loses.

canon.title: He Would Not Go In Without the Dog
canon.value: who you will not leave behind
canon.hook: Yudhiṣṭhira is offered heaven. He refuses to enter without the dog that followed him there.

canon.title: What Kuntī Came to the River to Say
canon.value: an apology that never comes
canon.hook: She waits until he has finished praying, and then tells him the one fact about himself that everybody has kept from him, on the day before the war.
canon.careNote: A mother tells a grown son, days before a war, that she gave him away at birth. He says she has come back because she needs something, and the story does not answer him. They then agree which of her sons will die.

canon.title: The Blade of Grass Kubera Couldn't Outweigh
canon.value: small things count
canon.hook: Kubera puts his treasury, his wife and his city on a scale. One offered blade of dūrvā still weighs more.

canon.title: The Night We Don't Look at the Moon
canon.value: owning what you did
canon.hook: There is one night in Bhādrapada when families are careful about looking at the Moon. This chapter tells why.

canon.title: Sāvitrī Follows Yama
canon.locus: Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya Parva, K.M. Ganguli CCLXLIII–CCLXLVI
canon.value: not stopping when told to
canon.hook: Yama tells Sāvitrī to turn back. She keeps walking beside him until his own boons change what is possible.

canon.title: Damayantī Chooses Nala
canon.locus: Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna Parva, K.M. Ganguli LIII–LVII
canon.value: the choice you make on purpose
canon.hook: Damayantī enters to choose Nala and finds five identical Nalas waiting.

canon.title: Sampāti Can Help Only With Words
canon.value: when your own strength runs out
canon.hook: The search party needs a direction. The bird who knows where Sītā is has no wings.

canon.title: The Ring in the Aśoka Grove
canon.value: what counts as real
canon.hook: Hanumān finds Sītā. Now he has to prove that a stranger in Laṅkā really comes from Rāma.

canon.title: Three Steps of Land
canon.value: a promise with no exceptions in it
canon.hook: A dwarf asks for three steps of land. Bali is warned those three steps may cost him everything.

canon.title: Ambarīṣa Waits for His Guest
canon.value: holding your ground politely
canon.hook: A king sips water to save a vow without eating before his guest. His guest returns furious.

canon.title: Maitreyi's Question
canon.value: refusing an easy answer
canon.hook: Maitreyi is offered a share of a household's wealth and asks one question: can it make me immortal?

canon.title: The Feast Kubera Could Not Finish
canon.locus: Modern oral/children's retellings; early textual locus unverified
canon.value: small things count
canon.hook: Kubera builds a feast to prove how much he owns. Gaṇeśa keeps eating until a few grains offered differently finally become enough.

canon.title: The Test at Vaikuṇṭha
canon.value: standing up gently
canon.hook: Bhṛgu provokes Brahmā and Śiva, then kicks Viṣṇu in the chest. The last response ends the test.
canon.careNote: Bhṛgu deliberately provokes Brahmā and Śiva, and kicks Viṣṇu on the chest. Śiva briefly raises his trident; nothing is described graphically.

canon.title: The Blade of Darbha in the Water Spout
canon.locus: Uṣāharaṇa-kāvya, Canto I; Skanda Purāṇa, Aruṇācala Māhātmya 6.51b–53
canon.value: a promise with no exceptions in it
canon.hook: Before Vāmana's three cosmic steps, Śukrācārya blocks a water-pot spout and one blade of darbha changes the gift.
canon.careNote: A blade of darbha pierces one of Śukrācārya's eyes while he blocks the water-pot. The injury is brief and not graphic.

canon.title: The Jewel Kṛṣṇa Was Blamed For
canon.locus: Skandha 10, chapter 56; parallel Viṣṇu Purāṇa IV.13
canon.value: looking at it before fixing it
canon.hook: A hunter vanishes wearing a jewel bright as the Sun. Before anyone follows the tracks, Dvārakā has already decided who took it.
canon.careNote: Prasena and his horse are killed by a lion; Jāmbavān kills the lion; Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavān fight for many days. The deaths and fight are stated plainly and not described graphically.
